title: Chapter 168 – What the Seven Remember
html:
[The Hall of the Sixth Door – Yue]

On the last morning but one, Yue packs a bag for the road, and discovers that she has nothing to put in it.

She stands in the little cell off the Annex corridor with her satchel open on the cot and looks at what she has. A slate. Three sticks of chalk. A spare smock, washed to the color of porridge. A coil of rope that Duan Ke gave her, with a hand-knotted loop at one end. A flask Bell filled with the black wax tea, which she will not drink. A square of oiled cloth to keep the rain off. Her cloak.

She turns the cloak over in her hands. It is the red one, the dull red of old brick, with a hole at the hem where a crawler's hook once took it. She has worn it since the valley. She thinks, suddenly, of her mother stitching it, a long time ago, with her tongue between her teeth.

She puts it on. She ties the satchel. She does not look for anything else.

The pebble is the only thing she wishes she could pack, and she cannot. It is where it has always been, against her breastbone, a small round weight under the smock. It is warm. It is silent. Forty-nine days it has been silent, and she has stopped waiting for it to speak, and she has not stopped listening.

A tap on the door. She turns.

Mo Yan is standing in the corridor with her hands behind her back and her charcoal stub clenched in her teeth. When she sees Yue's face, she takes the stub out of her mouth, and grins, and holds out her left hand.

Yue takes it.

Good morning, says the cracked silver bell in the back of her skull.

Good morning, Yue thinks, back. It is easier every day. What is it?

Cheng Hui wants us. All of us. He says it's important.

Now?

He says before the road. A pause, a faint wavering of the line. He's being a bit mysterious. I don't like it.

Yue smiles, and shoulders her bag.

* * *

Cheng Hui has laid it all out on the Annex table, with the cups cleared away and the ledger open at his elbow.

There are papers. There are three of Ethan's old pages, spread flat and weighted at the corners with Zhen Li's brass lamp, the rabbit, and Tao's top. There is a drawing in Mo Yan's hand of seven stick figures round a tree. There is the leather book, with its red silk marker. And in the middle of it all, drawn in fine black ink on a sheet of Nurse's best paper, is a diagram that Yue recognizes with a start: a ring of nine small circles, eight smooth, one scored.

She stops in the doorway. The room is full. Bell is by the stove with her arms folded. Nurse is at the window. Jian sits on the eighth cot with the staff across his knees and his eyes half closed, and the six children are gathered round the table in a ring. Duan Ke is on his feet. Hai Ren sits in the Great Stillness. Tao is on his knees on a stool, nose almost touching the paper.

Cheng Hui looks up as she enters. "Ah," he says. "The listener. Good. I was afraid you would not come."

What is it? she writes. She holds up the slate.

"A proposal." He taps the diagram. "And a favor. I am going to ask a great deal of you, and of Mo Yan, and I would rather you heard it before I asked."

Bell says, from the stove, in a low voice, "He has been awake three days and thinks he can do anything."

"I think I can do this." The scholar does not look round. "You have heard Mr. Cole. The Nine raised the Hall. They took a vow. They died, all but one, and the one has told us nothing. I do not blame him. But I have been reading his pages, and there is something I cannot make fit."

He lifts a sheet and holds it out to her. It is covered in fine brown writing. She cannot read it. The language is the old one.

"This is a copy of the seal," Cheng Hui says. "The thing that was written into each of us at the moment of our making. The pattern that lets the copy sit quietly, as he put it, in a child. I have read it eleven times." He sets it down. "It is not one seal. It is eight."

Yue frowns.

"Each of us is sealed differently. That much I had guessed. But what I did not understand until yesterday is why. The seals are not locks. They are vessels. Each Operator carries a piece of something. A portion of what Mr. Cole remembered on the night he made us." His dark eyes lift. "I believe we are the Nine's memory. All of it. Cut into eight slices, so that no single mind could carry the whole."

* * *

It is Hai Ren who says the thing that no one wants to say.

"You wish us to open them," he says, in his dry quiet whisper. "The seals. To pool the pieces. And you wish the listener to hear."

"Yes."

"It may harm us."

"It may." Cheng Hui does not flinch. "I have no doubt it will cost us something. The seal was made to hold a secret. When the secret is released, it may not be there afterward."

"We would forget," says Zhen Li.

"We would forget what we had remembered. Yes."

Zhen Li looks at his lantern. He has a hollow, exhausted look. "I've already forgotten so much," he says. "I'm not sure I'd notice."

Duan Ke has gone pale. "And what if it's bad? What if it's something we shouldn't know?"

"Then we shall have found out." Cheng Hui spreads his hands. "I do not propose it lightly. I propose it because we are about to leave the one place in the world that can answer our questions. Mr. Cole is silent. The stone is silent. The sleepers are silent. We are the only witnesses left, and we are not even aware of what we witnessed."

From the grille in the wall, very quietly, a voice says, He is right.

Everyone turns.

It is Mei, says the voice. I'm sorry to interrupt. Papa is asleep. He's been asleep all night, and I didn't want to wake him. A pause. I think it should be done. I think Papa wants it to be, even though he can't say so.

"Why?" asks Nurse. Her voice is sharp.

Because he has been carrying it too long. The thin voice steadies. Because I can feel it, in his hands. He holds me, and he holds it, and the weight of the second is breaking him. If you take it from him, even for an hour, I think he might rest.

Nobody speaks. Bell's arms have loosened. Nurse has turned from the window.

"Then it is decided," says Cheng Hui softly. "If the Ninth Voice consents."

I consent, says Mei. And I'm sorry. I think this is going to hurt.

* * *

Bell takes Cheng Hui aside before the ring is made, and her voice is not low.

"You will not do this to a three-year-old," she says.

"Ao has agreed."

"Ao is three. He does not know what agreed means."

"Then we shall explain it." The scholar does not raise his voice. "Madam, I have the greatest respect for your craft. But I would ask you to consider what you are choosing between. On the one side, the risk that a child may lose a memory he cannot name. On the other, the certainty that we walk out of this Hall blind."

"A child may lose a great deal more than a memory."

"He may." Cheng Hui looks across the room, to where Ao sits on the stool with the rabbit in his lap and his eyes huge. "Or he may lose nothing. I cannot tell you. But I will tell you what I believe. I believe he would want to. He asked me last night what was in the box in his head. I said I did not know. He said that he would like to find out."

Bell's face tightens. She looks at the little boy. He looks back, with the grave patience of the very young, and gives her a small solemn nod.

She exhales through her nose.

"I will be sitting at your elbow," she says to Cheng Hui, very low. "The moment any of them cries out, I stop it. I do not care what you have said. Is that understood?"

"Perfectly."

"And if the girl bleeds, I stop it."

"I would expect nothing less."

"Good." She turns away, then back. "You are an infuriating young man."

"So I have been told," says Cheng Hui, and bows.

* * *

They sit in a ring on the Annex floor, with their hands joined.

Ao is on Yue's left, Tao on her right. The small hands are warm in hers, Ao's damp, Tao's rough. Beyond them Zhen Li, Hai Ren, Duan Ke, Cheng Hui, and, at the farthest point of the circle, directly across, Mo Yan, cross-legged, her charcoal stub in one fist and her other hand stretched out across the gap to Yue's.

Not a ring, she realizes. A line, bent into a ring. A chain with the listener at one end and the first of the seven at the other.

Bell crouches beside Jian on the cot. Nurse holds the lamp. Behind them, in the shadow by the door, stands a figure Yue did not expect: the boy in the white smock, standing very straight, hands clenched at his sides.

The eighth. The little one.

He is the lock, Cheng Hui had said, earlier, quietly. He is the one the seals are keyed to. Without him it will not open.

Yue looks at him across the room. He looks back. He lifts a hand, once, in a small, serious wave, and she lifts hers.

"Begin," says Cheng Hui. His voice is steady. "Mo Yan?"

The girl nods. She shuts her eyes.

And the world falls silent.

* * *

It is not the silence Yue knows.

Her own silence is a country. It has weather and roads. It has the throb of the floor and the slap of a door and the pulse in her throat. But this is a different silence, deeper and darker, and in it the silver line rises, wavering, bright. It runs out of Mo Yan's hand into hers, up her arm, into her skull. It spreads across the dark like frost across a window.

Then it begins to sing.

She has never heard a song. She has never heard a voice raised in music, nor the sound of a lute, nor the hum of a mother over a cradle. But there is a shape in the line, a series of rising and falling curves, and her mind turns them into something that is almost sound. A low chord. A high thread. A beat like a heart. It is not hearing. It is the idea of hearing, laid over the dark like a map.

And then the first voice speaks.

Is everyone here?

It is a man's. It is clear, tired, and unmistakably Ethan's, but much younger than the one she has met. It is the voice of a man of thirty, scared and trying to hide it. It comes from nowhere. It fills the whole of the dark.

Nine, says another, a woman's voice, calm and low. We have nine. I counted twice.

Good. Sit, please. I've made tea.

A laugh. Several laughs.

You made tea, says a deep, rough voice. At the end of the world. Typical.

I couldn't think of anything else to do.

The darkness thins. A shape forms in it, not a picture but a pattern of silver lines: a round table. Nine chairs. Nine figures seated at it, indistinct, drawn in light.

* * *

She learns them one by one.

The woman who counted twice is Ma Ruo-lin, who can hold a mountain still. Yue knows it, somehow, from the tilt of the silver outline, the stolid weight of the shoulders. The deep rough voice belongs to a man the others call Old Brenn, and he can sing a fever down. There is a young man named Kito, thin and quick, who sits cross-legged on his chair and keeps getting up to pace, and who can see what is going to happen and is never wrong. There is a woman called the Cartographer, and a man called the Ferryman, and a small silent person in a veil, and two more whose names the memory has worn smooth.

And at the foot of the table, hunched over a cup of tea, is the ninth.

We all know why we're here, says Ethan. I'll say it anyway. So it's said.

The silver figures are still.

The Seam is rising. His voice shakes. Not a surge. Not a season. The whole river is coming up. In sixty years it'll breach the crust, and everything above will go. Cities. Mountains. Seas. The beasts will have the world. A pause. I've run the numbers four hundred times. I wanted to be wrong.

You are not wrong, says Kito. His voice is soft. I saw it when I was nine.

We have a plan. This is Ma Ruo-lin. We have had it for a year. I want to say it plainly, for the records. A rustle. There are nine places where the Seam runs close to the surface. We will build a Door at each. A seal of stone and will. A gate that can be shut from the dark side, and held there.

Held by what? asks the Ferryman.

By us, says the woman. Each of us will take a Door. We will make ourselves its keystone. We will stand in the gate until the tide has passed.

And then?

A long silence.

And then, says Old Brenn, gruffly, we will not be coming back.

* * *

Yue's hands are trembling. She cannot tell whether the tremor is in her body or the silver line. Ao's fingers are tight in hers, and she can feel him sobbing, silently, though she does not know when he began.

In the memory, nobody moves.

That is the plan, says Ethan. I'm sorry. I should have said that more gently.

No, says the Cartographer. It's the right way. People should hear it plain.

I have a daughter, says Ethan. I have to say it. I can't take a Door. If I'm gone, she has nobody. I have to ask you— His voice breaks. I have to ask whether one of you will take mine.

Silence.

I'll take it, says Kito.

Kito—

I'm nineteen. I'd have been dead by thirty anyway. I've seen it. The young man's laugh is light. Besides, I like your daughter. She told me a joke once. It was terrible.

It's not fair, Ethan whispers.

No, says Kito. But it's mine to give.

And the silver figure stands, and walks, and a door that was not there before opens in the dark behind the table. It is a tall door, black as basalt, with a seam of white light round its edge. He stops on the threshold. He turns his head.

One thing, he says. Ethan. Write this down.

I'm listening.

The Seventh Door is mine. It's the one under the valley, where you'll plant the tree. I'll hold it until the tree has fruited. After that, it can be opened from the valley side. The silver outline is smiling. You'll know when. The Rest of All will wake. Not before.

Kito, I don't understand—

You will. He lifts a hand. Tell her the joke wasn't that bad.

He steps through. The door closes without a sound.

* * *

The table is quieter with one chair empty. The silver outlines have shifted, closing the gap, and for a long moment nobody speaks. Then Old Brenn clears his throat.

And the Hall? he asks. We haven't said what to do with the Hall.

That's mine, says Ethan. He sets his cup down. The Doors will hold, if they're held. But there is a second problem. The Seam does not only open the ground. It opens the sky, for a time. The air goes bad. The seas go bad. Whoever is above will have nowhere to go.

So we put them to sleep, says the Cartographer.

So we put them to sleep. He draws a breath. The Rest of All. Whoever consents. Whoever we can reach. A hall, under the mountain, where the sleepers can lie until the tide has passed and the world has healed.

How long? asks the veiled one. It is the first thing she has said.

I don't know. A bleak little laugh. A century. A thousand years. I've never been able to make the number come out the same twice.

Who keeps it?

I do. The silver outline of his head bows. I'm the one who can't take a Door. So I'll take the Hall. It'll need a keystone. A mind to run it. I've been thinking about that.

A silence. Ma Ruo-lin says, quietly, Ethan.

I know what you're going to say.

You're going to put her in it.

I'm going to put a pattern in it. His voice cracks. A copy. Not her. She'll be here, with me, in the real world. It's only a backup. Just until the tide has passed. And then I'll take her out and she'll be all right.

Nobody answers.

It's what I'm good at, he whispers. I've got to do something.

In the dark, Yue feels the silver line tremble. She feels the hand in hers, Ao's, tighten convulsively. She knows what he does not: that the pattern in the Hall is not a backup, and never was, and that the real girl is the one in the hospital bed, whom the man in the memory will never see again.

She'll be a keystone, says Ma Ruo-lin, very quietly. Eleven years old.

I know.

She'll hold it for six hundred years.

Please don't, says Ethan. Please don't say the number.

* * *

When it ends, it ends all at once.

The silver line snaps. The dark shatters like glass. Yue is on her back on the cold floor of the Annex, gasping, with Ao's hand still clenched in hers and her whole body soaked in sweat. The lamps swim. There is a roaring in her skull that is not sound.

"Yue!" Bell's face swims above her, white and frantic. "Yue, can you hear me? Look at me!"

She cannot answer. She cannot see anything but silver, a cold shifting glitter across the whole of the room, like frost on a window at dawn. She turns her head and vomits on the boards, and Bell holds her hair.

Beside her, Ao is wailing. A thin, high, bewildered wail, the sound of a three-year-old woken from a nightmare. Tao is shouting something. Zhen Li is lying flat on his back with his eyes wide open and a tear running into each ear. Duan Ke is on his knees with his hands over his face. Hai Ren has not moved, but a line of blood runs from one nostril. Cheng Hui is holding his head in both hands and saying, over and over, Gone. It's gone. I had it just now. It's gone.

Mo Yan is the only one who is smiling.

She lies curled on her side with her charcoal stub clutched in her fist and a thread of red running from her nose into her mouth, and her eyes, wide and dark, are fixed on Yue's. Did you get it? says the silver bell, faint and cracked. Did you keep it?

Yue closes her eyes. She searches, in the dark behind her lids, for the table, and the nine chairs, and the black door. They are there. Every word. Every outline. The weight of Ma Ruo-lin's shoulders. The crack in Old Brenn's laugh. The terrible light smile on Kito's face as he stepped through.

Yes, she thinks. I have it.

Good. The bell is fading. Then it isn't lost.

* * *

The cost shows up in the small things.

Ao does not remember the lullaby. He wakes the next morning with the rabbit tucked under his chin, and when Nurse sits by his cot and begins to hum it, the song Operator Five used to sing, he looks at her blankly and says, "What's that?" She stops. She sits very still with her hands in her lap. After a while she says, "Nothing, sweetheart. An old tune." And she does not hum it again.

Tao has forgotten how to spin his top.

It is the most terrible thing that Yue has ever seen a child do. He crouches on the Annex floor with the little wooden toy in both hands and winds the string round it, and pulls, and it falls over. He winds it again. It falls again. His lip is trembling and his face is red, and he does not ask for help.

Yue sits beside him on the boards. She takes the top, very gently, and winds the string, and shows him with her own hands how the wrist turns and the string snaps. The top spins. It whirs, and wobbles, and slowly stills.

Tao looks at it a long time.

"I knew that," he says, hoarsely. "I knew that yesterday."

I know, Yue mouths.

He leans against her side, small and hot and furious, and says nothing more. She puts her arm round him, and the top spins, and spins, and slows.

* * *

She writes it all down that night, in the cell, by the light of a single amber lamp.

It takes her six hours. She writes on the back of Cheng Hui's fine paper, in her square firm hand, as fast as the chalk will let her, and when the paper runs out she writes on the wall. The Nine. The Doors. The plan. The names. Kito's last words.

The Seventh Door is the one under the valley, where you'll plant the tree.

She stops. Her chalk hovers.

She reads the line again. Her heart is pounding.

Where you'll plant the tree.

She thinks of the black bark, and the silver leaves, and Lin Jian's mother kneeling in the frost to feed the roots. She thinks of Qinghe's hands on the soil, and the stone circle at the edge of the orchard, and a hundred years of quiet.

She thinks: It was never just a tree.

She runs from the cell, with the paper in her fist.

She finds Jian in the corridor, in the dark, sitting on the floor with his back against the wall and the staff across his knees. He is awake. He has been awake all night, she realizes, listening for her. He looks up as she comes, and the lamplight shows the lines in his face, the gray in his beard, and the blue behind his eyes.

She holds out the paper. He takes it. He reads.

He reads it twice, with his lips moving, as an old man does who has stopped trusting his eyes. The lamp gutters. Somewhere above them a child coughs in her sleep, and settles. Then he lifts his head, slowly, and says in a voice she can read but cannot hear:

"Under the valley."

She nods.

"Under the tree."

She nods again.

His hands are shaking. The paper rustles. "My mother has been tending a door," he says. "For a hundred years. And never once knew it was shut."
